title: Yuma County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Yuma County wells have a 233-foot median depth. See local yields, water-level trends and modeled finished-well costs of $14,200-$24,800.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Yuma County
intro_html:
A well on land near Wray, Yuma or Idalia needs to be evaluated for both water supply and permitted use. Yuma County records include substantial stock and irrigation use, so a countywide yield figure is not automatically a household-well expectation.

Colorado DWR records contain 12,235 permitted wells in the county, with 5,510 recorded as constructed. Reported depths have a median of 233 feet, and reported pump yields have a median of 15.0 gpm. Those are useful starting points for a purchase or construction budget—not a guarantee for an individual parcel.

sections.heading: Budgeting for Depth Around Wray, Yuma and Idalia
sections.html:
Among the 7,653 permits reporting total depth, the median is 233 feet and the middle half fall between 140 and 303 feet. For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than treating the median as a fixed target. Ask how the price changes if the productive interval is deeper than expected. The 90th-percentile depth is 359 feet.

Ground here is alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name the Ogallala on 4,138 wells and the High Plains Aquifer on 124. Another 7,831 fall under an unnamed / fractured-bedrock label; that broad record category does not establish granite conditions on your lot. Local well logs near Joes, Kirk or Vernon are better guides to the formations a driller will encounter.

sections.heading: Yuma County Yield Numbers Need a Use Check
sections.html:
The 2,828 records with pump yields show a 15.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 10.0 and 50.0 gpm. Reported shares include 2% at 1-5 gpm and 0% under 1 gpm. That is encouraging for household supply, but it is not proof that low-yield or unsuccessful drilling cannot occur.

These are countywide records, not a domestic-only sample. The use mix includes domestic/household at 28%, stock at 41% and irrigation at 38%; those categories should not be treated as mutually exclusive. A reported pump yield also is not a sustained-output guarantee. For a home purchase, have the well's pumping performance, recovery and pump condition checked against the property's intended demand.

sections.heading: Recent Water-Level Records Point Deeper
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the bottom of the well. Yuma County's 556 reported measurements have a 121-foot median, with the middle half between 72 and 180 feet below ground. Do not subtract that median from the county's median well depth to estimate available water in a particular well; the measurements are not necessarily paired.

The decade medians became shallower from 145 feet in the 1950s to 91 feet in the 1990s, then deepened to 121 feet in the 2000s, 142 feet in the 2010s and 156 feet in the 2020s. The recent sequence suggests declining groundwater levels in the recorded sample. Different wells were measured across decades, however, so it does not establish a decline rate for your parcel.

sections.heading: A Long Drilling Record Across Yuma County
sections.html:
Permit issuance reached 1,565 in the 1970s, compared with 542 in the 1960s and 760 in the 1980s. Records show 816 permits in the 2010s and 371 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The current decade is incomplete in this dataset, so that comparison alone does not establish a slowdown.

The leading drillers in the records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc (Twiss, Raymond L.) with 1,814, Burgess Well Company Inc. (Burgess, Larry) with 435, and Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 390. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Ask prospective drillers about recent work near your parcel and request an itemized scope.

sections.heading: What a New Yuma County Well May Cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for drilling through alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 233-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $8,200-$12,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $14,200-$24,800.

Treat those amounts as planning figures, not contractor quotes. The 140-303-foot middle-half depth range leaves meaningful room for the actual drilled footage to change. Access, casing and grout requirements, pump selection and the route to the house also affect the scope. Before comparing bids, ask what each includes, how additional footage is charged and what you would owe if the hole does not produce an adequate supply.

sections.heading: Water Quality and Site Risks to Check Before Closing
sections.html:
The environmental map flags 74 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles of the county coverage. A mapped sampling location is not proof that a nearby domestic well is contaminated. It is a reason to review the underlying site information and discuss appropriate laboratory testing rather than assuming clear-looking water is safe.

Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage, and obtain a current water-quality test for a purchase. The reported 0% share under 1 gpm does not measure dry-hole risk or guarantee future performance. For a build, coordinate the well location with septic siting, house placement and construction access before excavation. Poor layout can complicate both sanitary protection and future well service.

sections.heading: Buying a Lot Near Eckley, Laird or Vernon
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit and construction record, then compare nearby wells serving a similar use. A productive irrigation well nearby does not establish either household-well yield or permission to irrigate your lot. Confirm that the existing or proposed permit allows the household, livestock and outdoor uses you actually need; exempt household-use permits can restrict outdoor use.

For an existing well, request pumping-test information, current water levels, water-quality results and repair records. For vacant land, verify permit eligibility before committing to a building plan. In over-appropriated basins, uses outside an applicable exemption may require augmentation. Countywide medians are useful screening tools, but records close to Eckley, Laird or Vernon should carry more weight than comparisons with Phillips County or Washington County.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Yuma County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported well depths in Yuma County have a median of 233 feet, with the middle half between 140 and 303 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 359 feet. Those figures come from 7,653 depth reports. Use nearby construction logs to refine a drilling budget; the county median is not a target depth for every parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Yuma County?
faq.a: The planning model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the county's 233-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $8,200-$12,800 and a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical at about $14,200-$24,800. Get an itemized bid that explains additional footage, completion materials and charges for an unsuccessful hole.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Yuma County?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gpm, and the middle half runs from 10.0 to 50.0 gpm across 2,828 reports. These records include stock and irrigation wells as well as household wells. For a purchase, test the actual well's sustained pumping performance and recovery instead of relying on the countywide median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Yuma County?
faq.a: The county data cannot establish whether an individual well is safe. Mapping identifies 74 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles, but proximity is not proof of contamination. Review nearby site records, inspect the wellhead and obtain current laboratory testing, including any additional tests warranted by local conditions.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Yuma County?
faq.a: Recent recorded decade medians suggest deeper groundwater: static water levels went from 91 feet below ground in the 1990s to 121 in the 2000s, 142 in the 2010s and 156 in the 2020s. These are different measurement groups, not a continuous record from the same wells. Check repeat measurements for the property before drawing a parcel-specific conclusion.
